Desktop from ui-components holds floating windows, DesktopWindow, which are not modal: many at once, as on the desktop of an operating system. A click in a window brings it to the front; the others stay behind as they were. Drag a window by its title bar, with the mouse, a pen or a finger; a double click on the title bar folds the window to it, and unfolds it again. The buttons of the title bar minimize the window to the taskbar and maximize it to the whole desktop, as each window allows, and its edges and corners resize it. While the focus is in a window, F11 maximizes it and restores it, and Ctrl+F6 and Ctrl+Shift+F6 go round the windows.

The taskbar has a button for each window: it brings the window to the front, restoring it when minimized, and minimizes the one already in front. While the window in front is maximized, the one you bring to the front is maximized too and takes its place. The buttons at the end of the taskbar tile the windows in a grid, side by side or one above the other, or cascade them; the last one lets the desktop fill the whole page, and takes it back into the page (Escape on the taskbar does too). Drag the taskbar, by its grip or where it has no button, to another side of the desktop, or press an arrow key on its grip: the windows move and shrink to stay on the desktop.

The windows hold the grids of the JSON Grid and Bean Grid demos, the same panels with the same actions: move their columns by drag and drop, resize them, edit, add and delete users in the overlay of the grid. The JSON grid is there three times, in Wicket, in React and in Svelte. The drop-downs of the Dropdown demo are there in Wicket, React and Svelte too. The React and Svelte tabs have desktops of their own, with the JSON grid, notes and the drop-downs of the framework, and six more of its demos, each in a window: Autocomplete, Buttons, Date and time pickers, JSON Infinite List, Modal Dialog and Progress Bar.

Every window can be closed. The menu of the taskbar, its button after the grip, lists the windows open, to bring one to the front, and those closed, to open one again; the button above opens the keyboard window too. Closing a window with changes not saved, a user being edited or drop-downs not sent, asks first: closing it anyway puts its fields back as they were.

With setSendToServer the browser sends via Ajax the states of the windows, the side of the taskbar and whether the desktop fills the page, each time you change them, and the sentence below the desktop follows; choosing another side for the taskbar above renders the desktop again, in the state you left it. Everything works under a strict Content Security Policy, without inline style. The desktop is a private component.

The windows are in panes, as in the workspaces of Ubuntu: the grids and the keyboard window in Grids, the drop-downs in Dropdowns. The buttons after those of the windows show another pane; Ctrl+Shift and the arrow keys go from pane to pane. + adds a pane, asking for its name, the pencil renames the pane shown (F2 or a double click on its button too) and the bin removes it, its windows going to the default pane, the first, which cannot be removed. The first button on the right of each title bar moves its window to another pane, or to a new one. The launcher of the taskbar, the button after its menu, opens new windows of the types the page registers: notes, and Bean grids; closed, they are gone. The server keeps the panes too.
